content: Why does a lens make a picture appear on a screen? I think the glass catches the light, flips it while the rays are inside, and then throws the finished picture forward. Is the focus just the spot where that picture sits, or is something else happening?

The lens does not build or flip a picture inside itself. Each point on the object sends light in many directions, and the lens redirects part of that spreading light toward a corresponding point beyond the lens. A screen placed where those points come together intercepts the pattern. The focus is not generally the image location; it is where rays from a very distant object converge.

If every part of the object sends light everywhere, I suppose the top half of the lens must carry the top half of the picture. Why does the image not get scrambled when all those rays cross, and what decides how large the upside-down picture becomes?

Every small region of the lens receives rays from many object points, so no region owns one slice of the picture. The rays can cross without affecting one another. Their directions after refraction sort them into separate image points. Object distance and focal length determine image distance and magnification: for a converging lens, placing the object beyond one focal length produces a real, inverted image.

Then covering the bottom half of the lens should definitely remove the bottom half of the image, because those rays no longer have a path through. What is the reason demonstrations still show a whole image, and why does it only look dimmer?

Rays from every visible object point normally pass through both halves of the lens. Covering the bottom blocks some rays from every point, rather than all rays from the bottom of the object. The full image therefore remains, but less power reaches each image point. Its fine structure may also change because the reduced, asymmetric aperture alters diffraction and aberrations, not merely brightness.

More precisely, my “top half” description conflated pupil coordinates with object-field coordinates. For an off-axis object point, how do the chief and marginal rays determine the conjugate image point once the paraxial approximation fails, especially when coma displaces the centroid of the point-spread function?

Beyond the paraxial regime, there is no single intersection shared by all rays. The chief ray mainly identifies image position and field mapping, while marginal rays reveal aperture-dependent aberration. Their intercept distribution at the image surface forms the geometric spot diagram; wave propagation gives the point-spread function. With coma, one may define the image point by chief-ray intercept, peak intensity, or centroid, and those choices need not coincide.

For a finite-conjugate system with a fixed sensor plane, is stopping down guaranteed to improve perceived sharpness across the field, or can diffraction and longitudinal chromatic aberration shift the optimum aperture differently by wavelength? I would expect the answer to depend on the detector’s spectral weighting.

It is not guaranteed. Stopping down suppresses many geometric aberrations and reduces defocus blur, but enlarges the diffraction pattern. Longitudinal chromatic aberration gives each wavelength a different best-focus plane, so aperture changes their relative blur without aligning those planes. The optimum depends on wavelength-dependent aberrations, illumination spectrum, sensor quantum efficiency, sampling pitch, and the sharpness metric, such as polychromatic MTF at selected spatial frequencies.

If the lens has appreciable thickness, I’m unsure whether using the Gaussian lens formula with distances measured from the glass surfaces merely introduces a scale error or can predict the wrong magnification sign. Should object and image distances instead be referenced to separate principal planes?

They should be referenced to the front and rear principal planes. Measuring from physical surfaces generally causes more than a uniform scale error because the two offsets differ and may change as groups move. The sign of magnification follows the conjugate geometry and sign convention; careless surface referencing can indeed yield a misleading result near a focal condition. A ray-transfer matrix or cardinal-point model handles thick lenses cleanly.

What actually happens if I cover half of a magnifying lens while it is making an image? I am certain half the picture disappears, since one side of the glass must handle one side of the scene. Why do some diagrams claim every piece of the lens sees everything?

Half the picture does not normally disappear. Each object point sends a fan of rays toward the lens, and rays from that point pass through many regions of the glass. Either half can therefore contribute to every image point. Covering one half reduces the light in the entire image and changes the aperture shape, which can affect blur, but it does not simply crop the scene.

I picture the light lines as thin threads that stay separate until the lens bends them into matching bundles. What is a ray in the real beam, and why does blocking a small patch make the whole picture fainter instead of punching a matching hole in it?

A ray is a geometric model for the local direction in which light energy travels, not a separate physical thread. A small lens patch receives a contribution from nearly every object point and redirects each contribution toward its corresponding image point. Blocking that patch removes one portion of every point’s converging wavefront. Consequently, the whole image loses light, while diffraction from the altered opening changes how each point is blurred.

So a wider lens should always give a sharper image, because it collects more light and more pieces of the scene. What is the blurry circle people mention near focus, and why not make the opening as wide as the glass allows?

A wider opening admits more light and can reduce diffraction, but it also uses steeply angled rays that expose spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, and defocus more strongly. A point then becomes a finite blur patch rather than an ideal point. Narrowing the opening can shrink aberrational and defocus blur until diffraction takes over. Lens designers choose an aperture that balances brightness, depth of field, aberrations, and diffraction.

To separate those effects, suppose the system is diffraction-limited and illuminated incoherently. The aperture then sets the optical transfer function through the autocorrelation of the pupil. How does obscuring one semicircle alter the modulation transfer function compared with reducing the pupil diameter symmetrically?

A semicircular pupil produces an anisotropic optical transfer function because its overlap with a shifted copy depends on shift direction. The cutoff frequency can remain tied to the full extent along some directions, yet contrast transfer falls unevenly and the point-spread function becomes asymmetric. A concentrically reduced circular pupil preserves rotational symmetry but lowers the cutoff uniformly. Thus equal transmitted area does not imply equal MTF behavior.

For coherent illumination, the transfer function is instead the pupil function itself, so the asymmetry should preserve some spatial frequencies while changing phase. Is the resulting image distortion adequately described by a shifted complex point-spread function, or do edge diffraction and speckle make that characterization incomplete?

The complex amplitude point-spread function, the Fourier transform of the pupil including phase, fully describes a linear shift-invariant coherent system. A half-pupil does not generally create only a shifted version of the original function; it changes its shape and phase structure. Edge diffraction is already included. Speckle, however, depends on source coherence and scattering or roughness in the object and system, so a deterministic point-spread function alone may not predict a particular speckle realization.

I’m less certain about polychromatic, partially coherent classroom illumination. When the source’s angular extent is comparable to the pupil’s diffraction angle, is Hopkins’ transmission-cross-coefficient formalism necessary, or can an effective incoherent MTF predict the visibility loss from a half-covered lens within useful accuracy?

An effective incoherent MTF can be a practical approximation when source points are mutually incoherent and the observable is a broadband, low-contrast pattern, but it can miss coupling between object spatial frequencies. Hopkins’ formulation is appropriate when partial coherence materially affects image formation. For a classroom source, the choice depends on source angular distribution, spectrum, object coherence, and required accuracy; measurement or numerical propagation is often simpler than assuming either limiting case.

Why does a magnifying glass make letters bigger when I hold it close? I think the curved glass stretches the light picture the way a clear balloon stretches something seen through it. Is the enlarged picture actually inside the lens, or floating somewhere above the page?

The glass does not stretch a picture stored inside it. When the page lies closer than the lens’s focal distance, the lens bends diverging rays so they leave less divergent than before. Your eye traces those outgoing rays backward and locates a larger, upright virtual image behind the lens. No light actually converges at that apparent location, so the image is neither inside the glass nor a floating object.

If the bigger image is not really sitting there, what does “virtual” mean? It sounds like the eye is being tricked into seeing light from a place with no light. Why can I see that picture directly but cannot catch it on paper?

Virtual describes the geometry, not an illusion: the outgoing rays diverge, but their backward extensions meet at an apparent source point. Your eye contains another lens, which converts those incoming rays into a real image on the retina. A sheet of paper has no focusing optics, so placing it at the apparent source cannot collect the diverging rays into the same pattern.

I am sure moving the glass farther from the page should keep enlarging the letters, because there is more room for the light to spread. Why does the view suddenly turn blurry and then upside down instead, and what is changing at that point?

As the page approaches the focal point from inside, the virtual image grows and moves farther away. At the focal distance, outgoing rays are nearly parallel, so there is no finite image location. Once the page moves beyond that distance, the rays actually converge to form a real, inverted image on the other side. Your eye and viewing position may not accommodate that rapidly changing bundle, producing the blurry transition.

More exactly, I was treating linear magnification as though it varied monotonically with object distance across the focal plane. For a relaxed eye viewing a virtual image at infinity, how does angular magnification compare with the near-point convention, and which definition is appropriate when accommodation varies?

For a simple magnifier, the relaxed-eye angular magnification is approximately the reference viewing distance divided by focal length, conventionally 250 millimeters over the focal length. If the final virtual image is placed at the near point, the common approximation becomes one plus that ratio. Neither is universal: the appropriate reference should use the observer’s unaided viewing condition, actual near point, eye-to-lens spacing, and accommodation state.

With a thick aspheric magnifier, can the usable field be optimized simultaneously for distortion, lateral color, and astigmatism, or do those corrections inherently compete? I suspect pupil location and eye relief make the answer design-specific, but I’m unsure which aberration usually constrains the field first.

They can be improved together over a specified field, spectrum, pupil, and eye position, but not independently or without trade-offs. Aspheric surfaces strongly control monochromatic aberrations, while lateral color generally requires dispersion choices or multiple elements. The first field limiter is not universal: simple singlets often encounter astigmatism and field curvature, whereas wide-field designs may be limited by distortion, pupil wander, lateral color, or sensitivity to eye placement.

For an extended object under broadband illumination, would a wave-optical treatment change the predicted magnification itself, or mainly the resolvable detail and edge contrast? I’m particularly interested in the regime where geometric distortion is small but the polychromatic point-spread function varies appreciably across the field.

Geometric magnification remains the leading mapping between object and image coordinates, but wave optics can shift an operationally measured magnification when asymmetric, field-dependent point-spread functions move edges or centroids. More commonly, diffraction and polychromatic aberration alter resolution and contrast rather than the nominal scale. The measured result depends on whether magnification is estimated from chief-ray mapping, feature centroids, edge locations, or a fitted image-registration transform.

What does a camera lens actually do when it focuses on someone nearby? I think it zooms the glass slightly so the person's light picture grows until it lands on the sensor. Why does turning the focus ring make the background blurry even when the picture size barely changes?

Focusing usually moves one or more lens groups to change where rays from the chosen distance converge. That is distinct from zooming, which primarily changes focal length and image scale, although some lenses alter scale slightly while focusing. When the sensor lies at the nearby subject’s image plane, light from a distant background converges in front of or behind it, reaching the sensor as blur patches instead of points.

Is the sensor like a wall that catches the picture at exactly one good distance? I assume a sharp photo exists only where all the light from the whole scene meets together. What is different about the nearby person’s light and the background light?

The sensor is a receiving surface, but the whole scene does not converge to one place. Each scene point has its own image point, and points at the same object distance share approximately the same best-focus surface. Rays from nearer and farther objects enter with different vergence, so the lens brings them to different image distances. A flat sensor can coincide closely with only a limited range at once.

Then a small hole in front should make focusing worse, because it throws away the outer light needed to complete the picture. Why does closing that hole make more distances look clear, and why does it eventually make everything softer?

The outer rays are not required to complete the image; they add light and angular diversity. A smaller aperture narrows each ray cone, so a sensor displaced from exact focus intercepts a smaller blur circle. That increases depth of field. Closing the aperture too far makes diffraction significant: every point spreads into a larger diffraction pattern, reducing fine-detail contrast even at the nominal focus plane.

More precisely, I conflated zooming with internal focusing and treated the image as a single convergence point rather than a field of conjugate points. In a floating-element design, how do principal-plane motion and focus breathing interact when the object distance approaches the minimum-focus limit?

Floating groups change both optical power distribution and the locations of the principal planes as focus approaches the minimum distance. The required conjugate shift can therefore occur without moving the entire lens by the thin-lens amount. Because effective focal length, distortion, and principal-plane position may all vary, image scale changes during the focus pull. That focus breathing is design-dependent and can be reduced, though usually alongside constraints on aberration correction, size, and travel.

If entrance-pupil diameter is held constant rather than f-number, does the usual depth-of-field comparison across focal lengths still hold at equal subject magnification? I’d expect pupil magnification and non-telecentricity to matter, especially for close focus, but I’m uncertain how large the correction becomes.

At equal subject magnification, depth of field is governed most directly by magnification, effective aperture as seen from object space, and the accepted blur criterion. Holding entrance-pupil diameter is not equivalent to holding f-number when focal length changes. At close focus, pupil magnification enters the object- and image-side cone geometry, while non-telecentricity changes chief-ray angles. The correction can be substantial for asymmetric retrofocus, telephoto, or macro designs, but is modest for near-symmetric lenses.

When field curvature and longitudinal chromatic aberration place different wavelengths and field positions at different best-focus surfaces, is a single circle-of-confusion criterion meaningful? How should one choose a focus metric when perceived sharpness, sensor sampling, and downstream computational sharpening favor different spatial frequencies?

A single circle-of-confusion threshold is then only a coarse specification. A stronger metric combines polychromatic, field-dependent MTF with spectral weighting, sensor sampling, viewing conditions, and the intended processing pipeline. The chosen focus position might maximize weighted MTF over selected frequencies and fields, minimize a perceptual loss function, or preserve worst-case performance. Computational sharpening should be included cautiously because it can restore attenuated contrast but cannot recover frequencies lost to zeros, aliasing, or severe noise.
